bio_full: Hirsch was born in Hamburg, studied briefly at the University of Bonn, and served as rabbi in Oldenburg, Emden and Moravia before becoming, in 1851, rabbi of a small separatist Orthodox congregation in Frankfurt, which he led for nearly forty years and built into a model community with its own schools.

Against the Reform movement, which was revising Jewish law and liturgy, Hirsch taught that the Torah is divine and binding, but that observant Jews should embrace secular education and citizenship, a principle summed up as Torah im Derech Eretz. His Nineteen Letters on Judaism (1836) and his commentary on the Pentateuch remain influential in modern Orthodox Judaism.

name: William James
bio: American psychologist and pragmatist philosopher whose Varieties of Religious Experience founded the modern psychology of religion.
bio_full: William James, elder brother of the novelist Henry James, grew up in a cosmopolitan family shaped by his father's Swedenborgian religious interests. He trained in medicine at Harvard, where he taught for most of his career, first physiology, then psychology and philosophy. His Principles of Psychology (1890) was a founding text of the discipline, and with C. S. Peirce he developed pragmatism.

His Gifford Lectures, published as The Varieties of Religious Experience (1902), studied conversion, saintliness and mysticism through first-hand accounts, judging religion by its fruits in human life rather than by doctrine. The book remains a classic of religious studies.

name: Albert Schweitzer
bio: Alsatian theologian, organist and physician whose Quest of the Historical Jesus transformed New Testament scholarship; later a medical missionary in Africa.
bio_full: Schweitzer studied theology and philosophy at Strasbourg, became a renowned organist and Bach scholar, and taught New Testament at the university. At thirty he decided to study medicine, and in 1913 he founded a hospital at Lambaréné in what is now Gabon, where he spent most of the rest of his life. He received the Nobel Peace Prize for 1952.

His Quest of the Historical Jesus (1906) reviewed a century of attempts to write the life of Jesus, arguing that each had projected its own values onto him, and presenting Jesus as an apocalyptic prophet expecting the imminent end of the world. His ethic of 'reverence for life' was widely admired, while later critics have questioned the paternalism of his approach to Africa.

name: Martin Buber
bio: Austrian-Jewish philosopher of dialogue, author of I and Thou, who also brought Hasidic tales to a wide modern readership.
bio_full: Buber grew up partly in Lemberg (Lviv) with his grandfather Solomon Buber, a scholar of midrash, studied philosophy and art history in Vienna, Berlin and elsewhere, and became active in cultural Zionism. He taught at Frankfurt until the Nazis barred him and emigrated in 1938 to Jerusalem, where he was a professor at the Hebrew University and advocated a binational Arab-Jewish state. With Franz Rosenzweig he made a new German translation of the Hebrew Bible.

In I and Thou (1923) Buber distinguished the 'I–It' relation of use and experience from the 'I–Thou' relation of genuine encounter, in which God, the 'eternal Thou', is also met. His retellings of Hasidic stories shaped modern perceptions of Hasidism, though scholars such as Gershom Scholem criticised them as selective. His thought influenced Christian as well as Jewish theology, education and psychotherapy.

name: Karl Barth
bio: Swiss Reformed theologian whose commentary on Romans and multi-volume Church Dogmatics made him the most influential Protestant theologian of the 20th century.
bio_full: Barth studied under leading liberal theologians in Germany and became a pastor in the Swiss village of Safenwil, where the support of his teachers for German war aims in 1914 and his encounter with Paul led him to break with liberalism. His commentary on Romans (1919, rewritten 1922) made him famous. He taught at Göttingen, Münster and Bonn, was a principal author of the Barmen Declaration (1934) of the Confessing Church against Nazi control of the churches, and was expelled from Germany in 1935. From then until his retirement he was professor in Basel.

Barth's theology, called dialectical or neo-orthodox, insisted that God is known only through his self-revelation in Jesus Christ, not through human religion, culture or natural reason. His unfinished Church Dogmatics runs to over nine thousand pages. He influenced Protestant and Catholic theology alike.

name: Paul Tillich
bio: German-American Lutheran theologian who interpreted Christianity in dialogue with existentialist philosophy, psychology and culture.
bio_full: Tillich was the son of a Lutheran pastor, served as an army chaplain in the First World War, and taught at Berlin, Marburg, Dresden, Leipzig and Frankfurt. A religious socialist, he was dismissed by the Nazis in 1933 and emigrated to the United States, where he taught at Union Theological Seminary, Harvard and the University of Chicago, becoming widely known beyond academic circles.

His Systematic Theology used a 'method of correlation', relating existential questions to theological answers, and described God as 'being itself' and faith as 'ultimate concern'. The Courage to Be and Dynamics of Faith reached a broad public, and his thought shaped the dialogue between theology, art and psychotherapy.

name: Dietrich Bonhoeffer
bio: German Lutheran pastor and theologian of the Confessing Church, executed by the Nazis, whose prison writings reshaped modern theology.
bio_full: Bonhoeffer came from a distinguished Berlin academic family and earned his doctorate in theology at twenty-one. A year at Union Theological Seminary in New York (1930–31), including time at the Abyssinian Baptist Church in Harlem, deepened his concern for social justice. From 1933 he opposed the Nazis and the pro-Nazi 'German Christians', led an illegal Confessing Church seminary at Finkenwalde, and in 1939 returned from America to share his country's fate. Through his brother-in-law Hans von Dohnanyi he joined the resistance circle in military intelligence. Arrested in 1943, he was hanged at Flossenbürg on 9 April 1945.

His Discipleship (in English The Cost of Discipleship) contrasts 'cheap grace' with costly grace, and Life Together describes Christian community. His letters from Tegel prison, published after the war, speculated about a 'religionless Christianity' for a world 'come of age' and have been widely debated. He is commemorated by many churches as a martyr.

name: Martin Luther King Jr.
bio: Baptist minister and leader of the American civil rights movement, whose nonviolent campaigns and sermons drew on Christian theology and the Hebrew prophets.
bio_full: King was the son and grandson of Baptist pastors of the Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta. He studied at Morehouse College, Crozer Theological Seminary and Boston University, where he earned a doctorate in systematic theology. As pastor of Dexter Avenue Baptist Church in Montgomery, Alabama, he led the bus boycott of 1955–56 and then the Southern Christian Leadership Conference, organising campaigns in Albany, Birmingham, Selma and elsewhere. He received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1964 and was assassinated in Memphis in 1968.

King's thought combined the Black church tradition, the social gospel, the personalist philosophy he studied in Boston, Reinhold Niebuhr's realism and Gandhi's nonviolence. His sermons and writings, such as Strength to Love and the Letter from Birmingham Jail, made a theological case for justice and love of enemies that influenced liberation movements worldwide.

name: Pope John XXIII
bio: Italian pope who called the Second Vatican Council and wrote the encyclical Pacem in terris; canonised in 2014.
bio_full: Angelo Giuseppe Roncalli was the son of sharecroppers near Bergamo. Ordained in 1904, he was secretary to the bishop of Bergamo, an army chaplain in the First World War, and from 1925 a Vatican diplomat in Bulgaria, Turkey and Greece, where during the Second World War he helped Jewish refugees, and then nuncio to France. He became patriarch of Venice in 1953 and was elected pope in 1958, aged seventy-six, widely expected to be a caretaker.

Within three months he announced an ecumenical council to bring 'aggiornamento', updating, to the church. The Second Vatican Council opened in 1962; he died of cancer in June 1963 before its second session. His encyclicals Mater et magistra and Pacem in terris addressed social justice, human rights and peace. He removed language offensive to Jews from the Good Friday liturgy. Known as 'Good Pope John', he was canonised in 2014.

name: Medieval Jewish scribes and illuminators
bio: The mostly anonymous scribes and artists who produced illuminated Hebrew manuscripts such as the great Haggadot of medieval Spain and Germany.
bio_full: Medieval Jewish communities commissioned richly decorated Hebrew Bibles, prayer books and above all Haggadot, the books read at the Passover meal. Scribes were often Jews, while illuminators could be Jewish or Christian, working in styles shared with the Gothic art around them. Some names survive in colophons, but most artists are anonymous, and art historians identify them by workshop and region.

These manuscripts, many of which survived expulsions and persecutions through extraordinary journeys, are among the treasures of Jewish art. They show that the biblical prohibition of images was understood to permit narrative illustration of sacred books, though some, such as the Birds' Head Haggadah, avoid showing human faces.
